findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Report & Accounts 2025 2026
findings.headline: Joanne Griffiths has been appointed Head of Pensions, succeeding Alex Bull, who left the Fund in March

findings.matters: A change of senior pensions officer is relevant to finance directors at other councils, both as a governance change and as a point of continuity for pooling and valuation work.
findings.figures: Not applicable

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Report & Accounts 2025 2026
findings.headline: The Local Pension Board reports that the McCloud implementation deadline may be extended to 31st August 2026
findings.detail: The Board was consulted on the discretion to extend the deadline for completing the McCloud implementation to 31st August 2026. The paper describes McCloud as a complex national LGPS administration project.
findings.matters: Finance and pensions teams at other councils working on the same national McCloud remedy can compare their own completion dates with the extended deadline.
findings.figures: Deadline for McCloud implementation extended to 31st August 2026 (discretion under consultation)
findings.quote: discretion to extend the deadline for completing the McCloud implementation to 31st August 2026

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Report & Accounts 2025 2026
findings.headline: The 2025/26 internal audit of the Fund's administration function gave full (absolute) assurance
findings.detail: The paper says the Head of Audit and Procurement provided full (absolute) assurance that the internal control environment was sound. It also says no significant governance issues relating specifically to the Fund were reported in 2025/26.
findings.matters: A clean internal audit opinion on a pension administration function is a control result that finance directors at other councils can compare with their own audit outcomes.
findings.figures: Full (absolute) assurance; no significant governance issues reported in 2025/26
findings.quote: full (absolute) assurance was provided

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Report & Accounts 2025 2026
findings.headline: The Fund's net assets were £5.05bn at 31 March 2026, with £186.169m paid to pensioners and £188.111m of total contributions
findings.detail: The overview table shows 69,078 scheme members alongside net assets of the Fund, payments to pensioners and total contributions for the year. The paper gives these figures without further commentary in the overview.
findings.matters: Net assets against annual pension payments and contributions show the scale of the Fund's cash flows, which a finance director at another council can use as a benchmark.
findings.figures: Net assets £5.05bn; payments to pensioners £186.169m; total contributions £188.111m; 69,078 scheme members

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Report & Accounts 2025 2026
findings.headline: Employer contribution rates reduced for many scheme employers following the 2025 valuation
findings.detail: The paper states that the improved funding position enabled contribution rates to be reduced for many scheme employers. The reduction is said to depend on each employer's individual circumstances.
findings.matters: Employer contribution rates are a recurring cost for councils and other scheme employers, so a finance director at another council can compare what happened to rates after a valuation with a surplus.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the paper
findings.quote: reduced for many scheme employers, subject to their individual circumstances.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Report & Accounts 2025 2026
findings.headline: The 2025 actuarial valuation reports the Fund's funding level rising from 97% in 2022 to 134% in 2025
findings.detail: The paper says the valuation confirmed a marked improvement in the Fund's financial position and a funding surplus of £1.135 billion. The S151 officer describes this as strengthening the Fund's ability to meet its pension obligations.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare this funding trajectory with their own fund's valuation outcome, and a lender can see that the Fund's liabilities are reported as well covered at the 2025 valuation.
findings.figures: Funding level 97% (2022) and 134% (2025); funding surplus £1.135 billion
findings.quote: with the funding level increasing from 97% in 2022 to 134% in 2025

findings.detail: The paper states that no decisions on changes to the investment strategy have yet been made. The initial phase of modelling is largely complete, and the Fund's advisers are reviewing and challenging the outputs before final recommendations are presented.
findings.matters: The timetable sets when the Fund's revised allocation and objectives will be fixed, and it is the timetable other funds in the pool will be working to.
findings.figures: December 2026; March 2027

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 08 - 2026 Investment Strategy Review Update
findings.headline: WPP IM Co became the FCA-authorised asset management company for the eight Welsh partner funds on 1 September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says WPP IM Co is now responsible for providing principal investment advice to partner funds and implementing agreed strategies on their behalf. As a result, the scope of this review is narrower than the 2023 review, covering the administering authority's remaining responsibilities.
findings.matters: Under the new pooling framework, a council's strategy must be advised by its pool, and the council's own role shifts to setting objectives and high-level allocation, which matters to any council in a pool.
findings.figures: 1 September 2026; eight Welsh partner funds
findings.quote: WPP IM Co is now also responsible for providing principal investment advice to

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 08 - 2026 Investment Strategy Review Update
findings.headline: The review identifies liquidity as a focus, with private market commitments and benefit payments that exceed contributions.
findings.detail: The paper lists the need to maintain adequate liquidity among areas for further consideration, alongside reliance on listed equities and the role of credit. Officers and WPP IM Co are developing a liquidity framework covering projected private market drawdowns and portfolio income. The paper describes the Fund as projected to enter a structurally negative cash flow position in the current year.
findings.matters: A fund with growing cash outflows and private market commitments to meet must plan how it funds them, and other funds with maturing memberships face the same question.
findings.quote: the need to maintain adequate liquidity to support private market commitments

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 08 - 2026 Investment Strategy Review Update
findings.headline: The Fund generated a cumulative return of 18.1% over the valuation period, equivalent to 5.65% per annum.
findings.detail: The paper says this exceeded the long-term return assumptions behind the previous valuation and contributed to eliminating the shortfall and creating a surplus. It credits an overweight exposure to global equities, strong US markets and a strong USD relative to GBP.
findings.matters: Returns above the assumptions used at valuation are a direct driver of the surplus, and the paper links that same equity exposure to the concentration risk the review is now testing.
findings.figures: 18.1%; 5.65% per annum
findings.quote: a cumulative return of 18.1%, equivalent to an annualised return of 5.65% per annum.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 08 - 2026 Investment Strategy Review Update
findings.headline: The Fund's funding level rose from 97% at the 2022 valuation to approximately 134% at the 2025 valuation.
findings.detail: The paper says the 2025 actuarial valuation confirmed a funding level of approximately 134%, an improvement of 37 percentage points over the three-year valuation period. It attributes the improvement to investment performance and to higher interest rates reducing the present value of liabilities. The Fund was in a modest deficit at the 2022 valuation.
findings.matters: A fund that moved from a deficit to a surplus is now reviewing its strategy from a different starting point, and the paper states the review's purpose is 'not simply to reduce risk'.
findings.figures: 97%; approximately 134%; 37 percentage points
findings.quote: approximately 134%, representing an improvement of 37 percentage points over the

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 11 - Wales Pension Partnership Update
findings.headline: The WPP's inaugural All-Wales Impact Report records £139 million invested across 97 assets in Wales, about 14% of WPP's UK investments.
findings.detail: The report, produced with The Good Economy and covering private market investments as at 31 March 2025, records £185 million committed to Wales-focused investments. Clean energy accounts for 67% of Welsh investments, and 63% are held through funds where WPP has a leading or influential ownership position.
findings.matters: Finance directors weighing local investment commitments against pooled return targets can compare the Welsh share of private market exposure and how it is measured.
findings.figures: £185 million committed; £139 million invested across 97 assets; approximately 14% of WPP's UK investments; 67% clean energy; 63% held with leading or influential ownership
findings.quote: £139 million invested across 97 assets in Wales

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 11 - Wales Pension Partnership Update
findings.headline: WPP IM Co had 16 permanent staff and two contractors in post, with two further appointments accepted.
findings.detail: The paper says recruitment is substantially complete, including a Head of Investment Operations, a Director of Operations and a Director of People, and the executive team is fully recruited. An Independent Chair and Non-Executive Directors have also been appointed.
findings.matters: Staffing is the operational capacity behind the pool's implementation role, and a finance officer at another council can see how far the company has got in filling its regulated structure.
findings.figures: 16 permanent staff; two contractors; two further accepted appointments
findings.quote: 16 permanent staff and two contractors currently in post

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 11 - Wales Pension Partnership Update
findings.headline: WPP IM Co formally commenced regulated operations on 1 st September 2026 after FCA authorisation.
findings.detail: The paper says the company's permanent Board convened for the first time on 2 September 2026, and the implementation services agreement was executed on 27 August 2026. Contract novations, service level agreements and a five-year business plan for shareholder approval in Spring 2027 remain outstanding.
findings.matters: The regulated investment management company now carries implementation for all Welsh pool funds, so a finance director at any partner council needs to know when it went live and which transition items remain open.
findings.figures: 1 st September 2026 (commencement); 27 th August 2026 (implementation services agreement); Spring 2027 (five-year business plan)
findings.quote: The Company formally commenced regulated operations on 1 st September 2026 following receipt of FCA authorisation.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 11 - Wales Pension Partnership Update
findings.headline: Torfaen's Fund had £4.16bn, 76% of its assets under management, invested through the Wales Pension Partnership as at 30 June 2026.
findings.detail: The paper reports the Fund's pooled assets with the WPP as at 30 June 2026 and lists 18 sub-funds, from Global Opportunities at £901m to Infrastructure (UK Sleeve) at £14m. The largest single holding is the Aquilla Life WPP World ESG Insights Equity Fund at £1,112m.
findings.matters: A finance director at another Welsh or English pooling authority can compare the 76% pooled share and the concentration in a single passive equity holding against its own pool arrangements.
findings.figures: £4.16bn (76% of AuM); Aquilla Life WPP World ESG Insights Equity Fund £1,112m; Global Opportunities £901m
findings.quote: approximately £4.16 billion, representing 76% of the Fund’s assets under management, was invested through the Partnership.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - Appendix 2 - ISA260 Greater Gwent (Torfaen) Pension Fund
findings.headline: The Wales Pension Partnership took over control and management of local pension funds’ investment assets from 1 April 2026, after the fund's assets were still managed locally at 31 March 2026.
findings.detail: The Wales Pension Partnership was developed into an FCA-regulated investment management company following the 'Fit for the Future' consultation. The auditor raised a risk over disclosure of the transition and agreed additional narrative in Notes 6 and 24.
findings.matters: Every Welsh local government pension fund faces the same transfer of investment control, so other councils' finance officers will want to see how the disclosure was handled.
findings.figures: Transfer date 1 April 2026; assets managed locally at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: took over control and management of local pension funds’ investment assets

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - Appendix 2 - ISA260 Greater Gwent (Torfaen) Pension Fund
findings.headline: Greater Gwent (Torfaen) Pension Fund held £9.2m with Bridges Fund Management at 31 March 2026 without a controls assurance report, which the auditor recommends obtaining from all fund managers.
findings.detail: The auditor's recommendation is rated Medium priority and was accepted in full by management. The fund says the manager decides whether to commission such a report, and it will raise the point with the Wales Pension Partnership and seek alternative evidence. The implementation date is March 2027.
findings.matters: Funds that rely on manager assurance reports to oversee investments will face the same question if a manager does not commission one, and the fix is due by March 2027.
findings.figures: £9.2m held with Bridges Fund Management; implementation date March 2027
findings.quote: As at 31st March 2026, GGPF held £9.2m with Bridges Fund Management.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - Appendix 2 - ISA260 Greater Gwent (Torfaen) Pension Fund
findings.headline: Audit Wales intends an unqualified opinion on the Greater Gwent (Torfaen) Pension Fund 2025-26 accounts, with certification aimed for 6 November 2026 and no uncorrected misstatements.
findings.detail: The report states that the auditor intends to issue an unqualified opinion once a Letter of Representation is received. It says there were no misstatements in the accounts, though five notes will gain additional narrative. The auditor is aiming to certify the accounts on 6 November 2026, ahead of the 30 November 2026 deadline.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council or a lender can compare the timing and outcome of this audit against their own certification deadline and opinion.
findings.figures: Certification target 6 November 2026; deadline 30 November 2026; reporting threshold £2.53 million; materiality £50.55 million
findings.quote: We intend to issue an unqualified opinion on the accounts

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - 2026 Investment Strategy Review Update
findings.headline: Fund reviewing diversification away from heavy equity reliance given improved funding position
findings.detail: Investment review is examining whether fund can achieve more efficient risk-return balance by diversifying away from high public equity exposure. Modelling assesses whether fund can continue meeting long-term return objectives while reducing equity concentration that proved beneficial when fund was in deficit.
findings.matters: A maturing fund with surplus position can reduce growth asset concentration, potentially improving resilience to equity downturns while still meeting return objectives.
findings.figures: Current high equity weighting being reviewed; specific new allocations to be recommended in December 2026
findings.quote: the Fund can continue meeting its long-term return objectives whilst diversifying risks (namely the high exposure to public equities)

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - 2026 Investment Strategy Review Update
findings.headline: Fund prioritising liquidity and cashflow management to support private market commitments and benefit payments
findings.detail: Investment strategy review has highlighted need to maintain adequate liquidity to support ongoing private market commitments and meet benefit payments exceeding contributions. Officers exploring how future investment income, portfolio liquidity and rebalancing arrangements can support requirements.
findings.matters: Liquidity constraints from maturing cashflow affect the types and illiquidity of assets the fund can hold and may constrain future private market allocations.
findings.figures: Specific liquidity framework under development; private market commitments and benefit payment requirements are the drivers
findings.quote: the need to maintain adequate liquidity to support private market commitments and benefit payments that exceed contributions

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - 2026 Investment Strategy Review Update
findings.headline: Wales Pension Partnership Investment Management Company assumed FCA-authorised responsibility on 1 September 2026
findings.detail: Government 'Fit for the Future' reforms have strengthened role of asset pooling and clarified responsibilities. Council retains responsibility for setting investment objectives, beliefs and high-level strategic asset allocation. WPP IM Co now has responsibility for detailed implementation, manager selection and portfolio management.
findings.matters: A shift in governance structure for investment management affects decision-making processes and accountability; it also clarifies the boundary between administering authority responsibilities and pool operator responsibilities.
findings.figures: Responsibility transfer date: 1 September 2026; applies to eight Welsh partner funds
findings.quote: Wales Pension Partnership Investment Management Company Limited (WPP IM Co), which formally assumed responsibility as the FCA-authorised asset management company for the eight Welsh partner funds on 1st September 2026.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - 2026 Investment Strategy Review Update
findings.headline: Pension fund projected to enter structurally negative cashflow in 2026 as membership matures
findings.detail: Underlying demographic profile is unfavourable, with pensioners expected to outnumber active members over time. Fund projected to enter negative cashflow in current year where benefit payments exceed contributions. Fund's surplus will need to compensate for faster growth in benefit payments relative to contributions.
findings.matters: A maturing fund facing negative cashflow must adjust investment strategy and maintain adequate liquidity; it will increasingly depend on returns and reserves to fund benefits rather than contribution income.
findings.figures: Negative cashflow entering in 2026; underlying issue is structural demographic imbalance in membership
findings.quote: Moreover, as with many LGPS funds, the underlying demographic profile is not favourable: over time, pensioners are expected to outnumber active members, which will exacerbate the structurally negative cash flow situation that the Fund is projected to enter in the current year.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 05 - 2026 Investment Strategy Review Update
findings.headline: Pension fund funding level improved to 134% from 97% over three years to March 2025
findings.detail: The fund moved from a modest deficit in 2022 to substantial surplus by 2025, with funding level improving 37 percentage points. Strong investment performance (5.65% annualised, 18.1% cumulative return) exceeded long-term assumptions. Improved financial market conditions reduced the present value of future liabilities.
findings.matters: A pension fund's financial position directly affects future contribution requirements and the council's budget; a move from deficit to 34% surplus significantly improves financial resilience.
findings.figures: 134% funding level at 31 March 2025 (up from 97% at 31 March 2022); 37 percentage point improvement; 5.65% annualised return; 6% actuarial discount rate required
findings.quote: The 2025 actuarial valuation confirmed a funding level of approximately 134%, representing an improvement of 37 percentage points over the three-year valuation period.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26 for Council
findings.headline: Council exceeded its interest rate exposure prudential indicator, holding higher variable-rate investments than approved
findings.detail: The council maintained average variable-rate investments of £18.722 million during 2025/26, exceeding the £15 million anticipated level in its prudential indicators. This increased the council's sensitivity to a 1% interest rate movement to £187,000 compared to the expected £150,000. The council acknowledges this exceedance in its key messages, noting it produced no adverse financial impact because actual interest rate movements were smaller than anticipated.
findings.matters: Exceeding formal prudential indicators shows the council's risk management framework was not followed, raising questions about control procedures and forecast accuracy—both relevant to credit risk assessment
findings.figures: £18.722m average variable-rate investments vs £15m anticipated; 1% interest rate sensitivity £187k vs £150k expected
findings.quote: The interest rate exposure indicator was exceeded, albeit it did not result in any negative implications for the Council, as explained within the report.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Report to Council - July 2026
findings.headline: Five-year programme assumes continued Welsh Government grant funding, but future allocations are uncertain and could be lower
findings.detail: The council's ability to keep external borrowing low and maintain the capital programme depends on unhypothecated grant funding from Welsh Government. The council explicitly notes that these annual allocations are determined by the Welsh Government budget process and there is a risk that future allocations could be lower than current levels, which would either reduce programme scope or force increased borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about external funding dependency that is outside the council's control, and whether lower grants would force unwanted borrowing or programme compression
findings.figures: £1.506m grant received 2025/26; total unallocated across 2027/28–2030/31 is 'just over £13 million'
findings.quote: the amount of unhypothecated funding (supported borrowing and General Capital Grant) for future years has been modelled in line with existing allocations. In reality, the annual allocations are determined as part of the Welsh Government budget setting process and, therefore, there is a risk that future allocations could be lower than the current year.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Report to Council - July 2026
findings.headline: Contingency falls to £240,000 on a £40.6m annual programme—just 0.6% coverage—after spending the Welsh Government grant
findings.detail: The council is committing the full £1.506m grant received in 2025/26 to capital schemes, reducing 2026/27 unallocated resources from £1.746m to £240k. The council describes this as 'adequate' for cost overruns or new pressures, but any material scheme slippage or price increase would exhaust contingency and force contingency to be brought forward from future years.
findings.matters: A lender would assess whether this level of contingency is sufficient to absorb the cost volatility typical in capital programmes, and whether the council can manage risk if multiple schemes overrun in the same year
findings.figures: £240k unallocated against £40.612m total 2026/27 programme; £1.506m committed to new schemes
findings.quote: In committing this resource to the priorities outlined earlier in the report, it will reduce the uncommitted allocation in 2026/27 to £240,000. This is felt to be an adequate level of resource in order to mitigate against the risk of cost increases against existing schemes or new pressures emerging during the remainder of the year.

findings.paper_title: Council Report - 2025_26 Governance and Audit Cttee Annual report
findings.headline: 2024/25 external audit of Statement of Accounts remains incomplete due to unspecified issues
findings.detail: The Committee has not yet received the ISA 260 audit report on the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts. The paper states this is 'due to issues identified which are being dealt with'. Almost a year after the financial year end, the external audit remains incomplete. The paper indicates resolution will occur 'during the current financial year' (2025/26), but no timeline or detail on the issues is provided.
findings.matters: Delayed external audit sign-offs with unspecified problems are a material concern for lenders. They suggest either issues with the council's financial systems, the accounts themselves, or both. Until the audit concludes, the 2024/25 financial position is not independently verified.
findings.figures: 2024/25 audit outstanding as of July 2026; planned resolution during 2025/26 financial year
findings.quote: The Committee has not yet received detailed reports on the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts including the ISA 260 (a report issued to those charged with Governance) for consideration due to issues identified which are being dealt with.

findings.paper_title: Head of Internal Audit Annual Report 2025_26 - July 2026 Governance Audit Committee
findings.headline: Community Hall Governance and Third Sector major grants audits show limited control effectiveness with less than 50% of expected controls operating.
findings.detail: Two audits received 'limited' opinions, indicating less than half of expected controls are operating as intended. These covered Community Hall Governance and Third Sector major grants. Follow-up audits are scheduled for 2026/27 to assess progress.
findings.matters: Limited control effectiveness in resource governance areas means the council may not be adequately monitoring allocation and use of community resources and grant funds.
findings.figures: Two audits with limited opinions; threshold is less than 50% of expected controls operating as intended
findings.quote: There were two audits in the year with a limited audit opinions i.e. less than fifty percent of the expected controls operating as intended by management. These related to Community Hall Governance and Third Sector major grants.

findings.paper_title: Head of Internal Audit Annual Report 2025_26 - July 2026 Governance Audit Committee
findings.headline: Elective home education service has two high priority control findings: applications not assessed within eight-week guideline, cases not reviewed annually
findings.detail: Applications are not being assessed within the eight-week guideline, and not all cases are being reviewed annually. These are statutory requirements for home education oversight. An action plan is in place with follow-up audit scheduled for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Failure to meet statutory timelines and conduct required reviews indicates regulatory non-compliance and potential capacity constraints, creating legal and reputational risk.
findings.figures: Two high priority recommendations identified
findings.quote: Both related to the Elective home education service which were previously reported to the Committee. The issues were that not all applications are assessed within the eight-week guideline and not all cases are reviewed annually.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outturn 2025-26 - Cabinet June 2026
findings.headline: Children's Services transition achieved without using most of allocated contingency, but this was exceptional performance unlikely to repeat
findings.detail: Children's Services was allocated a £1.986m transition fund to manage change and cost reduction. Only £53k was drawn, leaving £1.93m underspent. The report attributes this to 'the speed of change' in implementing a new operating model, reduction in placement numbers (438 budgeted, 427 actual), and vacancy savings. This one-off improvement underpinned the overall positive outturn.
findings.matters: While this year's improvement is positive, a lender should note it relied on exceptional pace of transformation and may not repeat; Children's Services remains a major cost base (£125.7m budget, nearly 51% of net budget).
findings.figures: £1.986m transition fund; only £53k used; placement numbers 427 vs 438 budgeted
findings.quote: However, the speed of change has been significant and meant that almost none of the transition budget was required. This resulted in a significant underspend against the Centrally Held Budgets line, which has underpinned the overall position.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outturn 2025-26 - Cabinet June 2026
findings.headline: Structural cost pressure on temporary homelessness accommodation where DWP subsidy does not cover full costs
findings.detail: The council recorded a £471k adverse variance against Housing Benefit Subsidy, with the report identifying this as a permanent feature: 'Housing Benefit costs that aren't eligible for HB Subsidy from the Department of Work & Pensions (DWP)' arise 'in relation to high-cost temporary accommodation for homeless individuals, where the DWP subsidy rate is fixed and doesn't cover the full cost incurred.' This is not a one-off or correctable issue.
findings.matters: This represents an unmatched cost exposure where statutory duties (housing homeless) generate costs that are not subsidised by central government at the rate incurred; it creates structural budget risk that cannot be externally resolved.
findings.figures: £471k adverse variance; described as ongoing scenario
findings.quote: Housing Benefit (HB) costs that aren't eligible for HB Subsidy from the Department of Work & Pensions (DWP). This scenario arises in relation to high-cost temporary accommodation for homeless individuals, where the DWP subsidy rate is fixed and doesn't cover the full cost incurred.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outturn 2025-26 - Cabinet June 2026
findings.headline: Capital programme experiencing persistent slippage, with £3.668m carried forward and limited contingency for cost overruns
findings.detail: Beyond planned slippage, the council identified £3.668m of unplanned slippage at year-end across projects including asset management (£739k), 3G pitches (£451k combined), and professional fees (£1.2m). The report explicitly warns that 'overall unallocated capital resources remain relatively low' and project managers must mitigate cost increases 'from within allocated budgets, or by seeking external funding, as much as possible.'
findings.matters: Persistent capital slippage and thin contingency indicate delivery risk on infrastructure investment and may signal planning or execution challenges that could delay service improvements or asset replacement.
findings.figures: £3.668m unplanned slippage; overall contingency described as 'relatively low'
findings.quote: overall unallocated capital resources remain relatively low and, as a result, project managers will need to mitigate cost increases that emerge from within allocated budgets, or by seeking external funding, as much as possible.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2025-26 and Revenue Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Recycling and Waste services under pressure: £302k adverse variance from agency staffing and reduced recyclate income
findings.detail: Neighbourhoods & Environment reporting £90k overall adverse variance, with Waste and Recycling services driven by £302k pressure. Main cost drivers: agency staff costs for collection services, plant repairs, and significantly reduced income from sale of recyclates (commodity market driven). Partly offset by vacancy savings elsewhere in service, but underlying cost base appears to have increased.
findings.matters: Rising waste disposal costs and reliance on volatile recyclate markets create structural cost pressures; high agency staffing suggests permanent staffing shortfall or contract redesign issue.
findings.figures: £302k adverse variance in Waste services; total Neighbourhoods & Environment adverse variance £90k
findings.quote: The main pressure area is in relation to Recycling and Waste services (£302,000) linked to agency staff costs, plant repairs and reduced income from the sale of recyclates

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2025-26 and Revenue Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Three schools forecast to close 2025-26 in deficit positions within school reserve envelope
findings.detail: School collective reserves forecast to reach £3.079m (3.71% of total school budget) by end of 2025-26, down from £4.731m previous year. Within this aggregate position, three schools have anticipated closing deficit positions. Council committed to 'close monitoring and support' throughout remainder of year, indicating emergent control and governance challenge in school financial management.
findings.matters: School deficits indicate control weakness in a major spend area and create future calls on council reserves through intervention, support, and potential restructuring costs.
findings.figures: Three schools in deficit; school reserves at 3.71% of budget (£3.079m); £1.65m reduction forecast in school reserves
findings.quote: contained within that overall position are three schools with anticipated closing deficit positions. Close monitoring of, and support to, the schools in deficit, as well as those at risk of entering a deficit position over the medium term, will continue throughout the remainder of the year

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2025-26 and Revenue Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: General Fund Balance declining significantly: £11.998m (2024) to forecast £9.205m (2026)
findings.detail: General Fund reserves falling by £1.7m year-on-year, with overall reserve reduction of circa £7.8m anticipated in 2025-26. While still above council minimums (£5.8m authorised, £7.5m operational), the consistent downward trajectory is concerning. Combined with school reserves falling to £3.071m and overall council reserves declining from £41.302m to £33.5m forecast, financial cushion is materially reduced.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's capacity to absorb unexpected cost pressures, service demand spikes, or income shortfalls, increasing financial vulnerability.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance: £11.998m (March 2024), £10.901m (March 2025 actual), £9.205m (March 2026 forecast); total reserve reduction ~£7.8m; school reserves forecast to £3.079m (3.71% of school budget)
findings.quote: General Fund Balance 11,998 10,901 9,205

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2025-26 and Revenue Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy gap creating permanent structural overspend with no funded solution
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation costs for homeless individuals continue to exceed DWP subsidy rates, creating £178k adverse variance at Month 7. £158k of the £517k total 'at risk' mitigations relate to Housing Benefit and are described as 'unlikely to materially change'. Council has factored this persistent pressure into 2026-27 budget, indicating expectation it will continue. DWP subsidy rate is fixed and does not cover actual costs incurred.
findings.matters: This is a demand-driven cost pressure with no fundable solution, reducing financial flexibility and exposing the council to unbudgeted costs driven by homelessness demand factors outside its control.
findings.figures: £178k Month 7 adverse variance; £158k at risk on 2025-26 mitigations; £414k estimated overall 2026-27 pressure (target reduction of £100k)
findings.quote: there continues to be an adverse variance as a result of Housing Benefit (HB) costs that aren't eligible for HB Subsidy from the Department of Work & Pensions (DWP), linked to high-cost temporary accommodation where the DWP subsidy rate is fixed and doesn't cover the full cost incurred.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2025-26 and Revenue Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £15.37m expected; only 41% spent despite seven months into year
findings.detail: Council's capital budget working base of £53.87m has £15.37m planned slippage carried forward. Major schemes affected include Pontypool Regeneration LUF (£5.4m), Sustainable Communities for Learning (£3.9m), The British (£3.5m), and Waste Transfer Station (£2.1m). Expenditure to date of only 41% despite scheme budgets typically weighted to second half of year suggests additional unplanned slippage likely by year end. Grant funding approvals will need to be sought for carried-forward schemes.
findings.matters: Capital delivery delays indicate project and scheme management challenges, potentially defer service improvements, and create uncertainty in asset deployment and debt servicing profiles.
findings.figures: £15.37m planned slippage from £53.87m working budget; 41% expenditure to date; major slippages: Pontypool Regeneration £5.4m, Sustainable Communities £3.9m, The British £3.5m, Waste Transfer Station £2.1m
findings.quote: the level of actual expenditure to date is circa 41% of the total budget... the level of spend currently achieved would suggest that additional slippage is likely to be identified by the end of the financial year. This slippage will need to be carried forward into 2026/27, in order to allow schemes to be completed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Prudential Indicators DRAFT
findings.headline: Council forecasts maintaining £15m investment balance throughout the planning period.
findings.detail: The Anticipated Investment Position shows the council expects to hold £15m in investments across all years 2025/26 through 2030/31, consistent with the Liquidity Risk target of £10m cash available within 3 months. This demonstrates sustained liquidity resilience across the planning period despite planned borrowing increases.
findings.matters: Sustained investment liquidity reassures lenders of debt servicing capability and shows the council can fund planned borrowing without depleting reserves.
findings.figures: £15m each year from 2025/26 through 2030/31
findings.quote: Investments 15 15 15 15 15 15

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Prudential Indicators DRAFT
findings.headline: Interest rate exposure of £540k per 1% rate move, with £390k on borrowing and £150k on investments.
findings.detail: The council's interest rate sensitivity analysis shows that a 1% change in interest rates would impact borrowing costs by £390k and investment income by £150k, totalling a £540k exposure. This exposure relative to gross borrowing of £128-138m indicates the council has limited floating-rate debt and is primarily hedged through fixed-rate instruments.
findings.matters: Interest rate sensitivity is material to debt service budgeting and refinancing risk; a well-hedged position with mostly fixed-rate debt reduces the risk of unexpected cost increases.
findings.figures: £390k borrowing cost exposure per 1% rate change, £150k investment income exposure per 1% rate change, £540k total variation
findings.quote: Interest on Borrowing 390,000 (390,000) Investment income 150,000 (150,000) Total Interest Variation 540,000 (540,000)

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Prudential Indicators DRAFT
findings.headline: Proportion of financing costs to net revenue forecast to improve from 3.66% to 3.48% then stabilize around 3.5% through 2030/31.
findings.detail: Despite planned borrowing increases, the council forecasts financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream declining from 3.66% in 2025/26 to 3.54% in 2026/27 and 3.48% in 2027/28, then stabilizing around 3.5%. This indicates the council expects to manage increased debt costs without proportionally higher revenue impact.
findings.matters: The financing cost ratio is a key measure of debt sustainability; a stable or improving ratio despite borrowing growth suggests sound financial planning.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Prudential Indicators DRAFT
findings.headline: Gross borrowing planned to rise to £137.79m in 2027/28 then decline to £129.71m by 2030/31.
findings.detail: The council forecasts an increase in gross borrowing from £128.01m in 2025/26 to a peak of £137.79m in 2027/28, before declining back to £129.71m by 2030/31. This indicates a planned expansion of debt funding for capital investment over the next two years, followed by a contraction. The Capital Finance Requirement shows the same profile, rising to £143.34m in 2027/28 then declining.
findings.matters: Lenders and peer finance directors need to understand a council's planned debt expansion and contraction to assess debt sustainability and capital priorities.

findings.paper_title: SemiAnnual TM Report 2025-26 For Audit committee DRAFT
findings.headline: Council under-borrowed by £12m relative to Capital Financing Requirement; maintaining £15m investment balance.
findings.detail: The council's forecast net external borrowing of £128m is £12m below its CFR of £142.83m, indicating use of internal cash resources to fund part of its capital programme rather than external borrowing. Investment balances are forecast at £15m year-end, held in short-term instruments (3 months or less). Minimum £10m is required for professional investor status under MIFID II.
findings.matters: The under-borrowed position reflects a strategic choice to use internal liquidity to reduce debt, but affects working capital available for operational needs; this balance between deleveraging and maintaining prudent reserves is closely watched by finance directors and lenders.
findings.figures: Forecast net borrowing: £128m; CFR: £142.83m; under-borrowed: £12m; year-end investment forecast: £15m
findings.quote: is currently under borrowed by £12 million with regards to its notional debt position.

findings.paper_title: SemiAnnual TM Report 2025-26 For Audit committee DRAFT
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased by £7.1m due to IFRS16 Leases accounting standard; actual borrowing continues to fall.
findings.detail: The CFR increased from £135.73m to £142.83m in 2025-26, entirely due to adoption of IFRS16 which requires leases to be capitalized. This technical accounting change does not represent additional borrowing need; actual external debt has fallen by £19.97m despite the higher CFR. Leasing costs are funded from revenue, not additional borrowing.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to distinguish between CFR increases from accounting changes versus real increases in capital needs, preventing misinterpretation of the council's true debt position and borrowing trajectory.
findings.figures: CFR 2025-26: £135.73m (original) to £142.83m (revised), increase of £7.1m due to IFRS16
findings.quote: The CFR has increased in 2025/26 as a result of the adoption of IFRS16 Leases, which is an accounting standard that requires the majority of leases to be treated as capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: SemiAnnual TM Report 2025-26 For Audit committee DRAFT
findings.headline: Capital schemes slipped: Waste Transfer Station, Levelling Up Programme, and The British re-profiled into 2026-27.
findings.detail: Three capital projects have experienced slippage and been re-profiled from 2025-26 to 2026-27. This has increased the 2026-27 capital budget to accommodate these delayed schemes alongside new grant-funded additions, indicating execution or planning challenges in delivering these projects on schedule.
findings.matters: Capital scheme delays affect service delivery timescales and push spend into future years, changing the capital profile and future borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: Schemes re-profiled from 2025-26 to 2026-27: Waste Transfer Station, Levelling Up Programme, The British
findings.quote: During 2025/26, there has been slippage on the Waste Transfer Station, the Levelling Up Programme and The British, with allocations for these projects having been re-profiled which has resulted in a budget increase in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: SemiAnnual TM Report 2025-26 For Audit committee DRAFT
findings.headline: Capital programme revised up by £9.88m in 2025-26 following award of additional grants for transport, prosperity, and coal tip remediation.
findings.detail: The capital expenditure budget for 2025-26 was revised from £28.62m to £38.50m, and for 2026-27 from £9.63m to £26.80m. The increase is driven by additional grant approvals including Active Travel Fund, Shared Prosperity Fund, and funding for coal tip work, representing a 34.5% increase in planned 2025-26 capital spending.
findings.matters: Additional grant funding expanding capital capacity improves the council's ability to invest in services and infrastructure without relying on borrowing, strengthening its financial position.
findings.quote: additional grants have been approved in 2025/26 such as Active Travel Fund (Transport), Shared Prosperity Fund and Coal tips.

findings.paper_title: SemiAnnual TM Report 2025-26 For Audit committee DRAFT
findings.headline: External debt reduced by £19.97m to £111.65m in six months; no new long-term borrowing undertaken.
findings.detail: Total external debt fell from £131.626m at end of March 2025 to £111.652m at end of September 2025. This reflects reductions in market loans (£24m to £23.75m), PWLB loans (£62.64m to £58.12m), and temporary borrowing (£42.5m to £27.5m). The council has taken no new long-term borrowing during this period.
findings.matters: A £19.97m debt reduction in six months demonstrates effective debt management and improving financial position, which lenders monitor as a key health indicator.
findings.quote: No new long-term borrowing has been undertaken year to date in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026_27 Audit Committee xx 2026 Draft (1)
findings.headline: Council pursuing asset rationalization and external grant maximization as primary levers to create capital headroom
findings.detail: With limited headroom for new borrowing, the council plans to 'subject [its] asset base to review, with a focus on optimisation and rationalisation' and notes 'there will continue to be a heavy reliance upon external grant funding.' This indicates capital receipts are insufficient and the council is dependent on factors outside its control (grant awards, asset sale values).
findings.matters: Over-reliance on discretionary government grants and unpredictable asset sales makes the capital programme fragile and exposes the council to cuts in national funding
findings.figures: Capital receipts £1.03m (2026/27); capital grants £19.81m (2026/27)
findings.quote: External funding should be maximised and used to pursue the Council's existing objectives wherever possible, rather than being used to pursue new initiatives at the expense of existing need and challenges.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026_27 Audit Committee xx 2026 Draft (1)
findings.headline: Significant unmet demand for capital, particularly school estate condition and Additional Learning Needs, may require revenue sacrifice
findings.detail: The council identifies 'significant issues within the school estate' and 'demand pressures, such as those within Children's Services and the growth in Additional Learning Needs.' It states it 'may not be possible to meet the full demand for capital expenditure' and may need to 'commit revenue resources for the purpose of new borrowing, however that would need to be balanced against other priorities.'
findings.matters: Unmet capital demand in schools and children's services represents a growing unfunded liability; any decision to fund it from revenue would further squeeze service budgets
findings.figures: £57m capital programme over 5 years (2026/27–2030/31) excluding resources to be allocated
findings.quote: It may not be possible to meet the full demand for capital expenditure and resources and, therefore, clear prioritisation of objectives will be key to ensuring the financial sustainability of the Council in the future.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026_27 Audit Committee xx 2026 Draft (1)
findings.headline: Revenue budget faces ongoing pressure from high interest rates and debt servicing costs amid reported in-year overspend
findings.detail: The council reports an 'in-year overspend position and the challenge in setting a balanced budget for 2026/27.' Interest costs and MRP (principal repayments) will consume 3.54% of the net revenue stream in 2026/27. The paper states 'interest rates remain high, which reduces the spending power of any revenue funding' and notes the council 'already has a need to externalise existing internal borrowing, which will come at a cost.'
findings.matters: In-year overspend coupled with rising borrowing costs signal structural budget difficulty and limited headroom for further financial pressure
findings.figures: Finance costs 3.54% of net revenue stream (2026/27); 2025/26 revised showed in-year overspend
findings.quote: It is important to recognise the challenging financial situation within which the Council is operating. This is evidenced within the revenue budget, given the recently reported in-year overspend position and the challenge in setting a balanced budget for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026_27 Audit Committee xx 2026 Draft (1)
findings.headline: Long-term external borrowing forecast to increase by £8.7m to refinance maturing temporary borrowing
findings.detail: Gross borrowing forecast rises from £128.01m (2025/26) to £136.75m (2026/27). The strategy notes this increase is 'largely due to the need to refinance current temporary borrowing and because of reducing internal borrowing capacity.' This means the council is running down cash reserves and will need to take on new debt at prevailing market rates.
findings.matters: Rising external borrowing increases interest cost exposure and refinancing risk; a lender needs to know the council is moving toward greater reliance on external funding
findings.quote: Long-term external borrowing is expected to increase, largely due to the need to refinance current temporary borrowing and because of reducing internal borrowing capacity.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026_27 Audit Committee xx 2026 Draft (1)
findings.headline: Capital programme reduced 30% year-on-year due to low resources and constrained borrowing capacity
findings.detail: The 2026/27 capital programme is £26.8m, down from £38.5m in 2025/26. The council explicitly states it has a 'relatively low level of its own available capital resources, diminishing capacity for internal borrowing, plus a limited ability to afford new external borrowing.' This reduction reflects fundamental resource constraints, not temporary timing.
findings.matters: Reduced capital investment signals financial stress and limits the council's ability to maintain its asset base or invest in service improvements, both of concern to lenders
findings.quote: The size of the programme is smaller than in previous years, which reflects the low level of capital resources available.
